text:
**Short answer:** Yes, at about $450-$500 or less, if you mainly want AC power for outages and camping and don't mind the weight. At the old $799+ prices, no.

**Buy it:** [BLUETTI AC180 (US store)](https://www.bluettipower.com/products/ac180?variant=44099774480603), listed at $499. Other sources show $449 on Amazon and at Bluetti's store ([iTechGuides](https://www.itechguides.com/bluetti-ac180-power-station-review-excellent-ac-efficiency-but-heavy-and-less-impressive-over-dc/), [Watt Power Station](https://wattpowerstation.com/power-stations/bluetti-ac180/)). Prices and stock vary by listing, so check the exact variant before you buy.

**What's good**
- **Real capacity:** Six independent tests measured 82-90% of the rated 1,152 Wh, or about 950-1,040 Wh usable ([Watt Power Station](https://wattpowerstation.com/power-stations/bluetti-ac180/)). PCWorld called its AC efficiency class-leading ([PCWorld](https://www.pcworld.com/article/1966571/bluetti-ac180-power-station-review.html)).
- **Power:** It puts out 1,800 W continuous and has a 2,700 W surge rating.
- **Battery and warranty:** It uses a LiFePO4 battery rated for 3,500+ cycles, with a 5-year warranty.
- **Charging:** A full wall charge takes about 1.3 hours in testing ([OutdoorGearLab](https://www.outdoorgearlab.com/reviews/camping-and-hiking/power-station/bluetti-ac180)).
- **Extras:** It has a 15 W wireless charging pad and app control.

**What's not**
- **Weight:** It weighs about 35-37 lb, which is heavy for its capacity. OutdoorGearLab scored it a middling 66 and criticized its power-to-weight ratio and noisy fan.
- **Small loads:** Efficiency drops sharply at low draw. One test got only 54% of rated capacity at 34 W, which matters for a CPAP or an overnight fridge.
- **DC efficiency:** PCWorld measured only about 71% on a USB-style DC load ([iTechGuides](https://www.itechguides.com/bluetti-ac180-power-station-review-excellent-ac-efficiency-but-heavy-and-less-impressive-over-dc/)).
- **Power Lifting mode:** The 2,700 W mode only works for resistive heating loads, not for everything.
- **Expansion:** Sources conflict. Bluetti's page mentions B80/B230/B300 expansion batteries, but Watt Power Station says it can only be topped up from them in Power Bank Mode, with no true expansion port.
- **Heat:** Output reportedly drops to 1,500 W above 95°F ([Best Batteries](https://us.best-batteries.com/reviews/bluetti-ac180/)).
- **Availability:** Some pages show discontinuation signals, so confirm it's in stock.

**Alternatives to compare:** OutdoorGearLab says its successor, the Bluetti Elite 100 V2, is better. It's lighter (25 lb), quieter, charges faster, and costs less on the street, with a bit less capacity (1,024 Wh). It also prefers the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2. Watt Power Station lists the Elite 100 V2 at about $489, the Anker C1000 Gen 2 at $499.99, and the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Classic at $499 (93% measured capacity). I don't have direct buy links for those from these results.

A third-party deal page, [Dealectric](https://dealectric.com/bluetti-ac180), says code AFF5OFF takes about $25 off at Bluetti's store. That page is an affiliate site, and checkout has the final word on whether the code works.

**Bottom line:** Buy the AC180 if it's $450-$500 or less and you want an AC-focused backup or camping unit. If weight, noise, or small-load efficiency matter to you, look at the Elite 100 V2 or the Anker first.
